title: Property-Based & Specialized Testing
summary: Example-based tests check specific cases you thought to write. Property-based tests, fuzzing, and snapshot testing check invariants across thousands of generated inputs — catching the edge case no human would think to hand-write.

slides.markdown:
Every test so far in this group is **example-based**: a human picks specific inputs (`convert(3) == "Fizz"`) and specific expected outputs. That's the right default, and it's also inherently limited by what the human writing it thought to check.

This topic covers three techniques that don't rely on a human enumerating cases: **property-based testing**, which checks an invariant holds across thousands of automatically generated inputs; **fuzz testing**, which throws malformed or random input at code specifically to find crashes and security holes; and **snapshot testing**, which captures output once and diffs future runs against it. Each catches a different category of bug that example-based tests structurally miss — and each has its own way of quietly stopping being useful if you're not careful.

An example-based test asserts a fact about one specific input: "sorting `[3,1,2]` gives `[1,2,3]`." A **property-based test** asserts a fact that should hold for *every* input in some space: "sorting any list produces a list that's non-decreasing and is a permutation of the original." The test framework then generates hundreds or thousands of random inputs — empty lists, huge lists, lists with duplicates, lists of negative numbers — and checks the property against every one.

The shift in thinking is from "what's an example that demonstrates this works" to "what's true about this function no matter what you feed it." That second question is often harder to answer, and answering it is exactly where property-based testing earns its cost — a well-chosen property can catch an edge case (an empty list, a single-element list, all-duplicate values) that never occurred to the author to write as an example.

slides.subTitle: Sorting is idempotent
slides.markdown:
```python
from hypothesis import given
from hypothesis import strategies as st

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_is_idempotent(xs):
    once = sorted(xs)
    twice = sorted(once)
    assert once == twice          # sorting an already-sorted list changes nothing

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_preserves_elements(xs):
    assert sorted(sorted(xs)) == sorted(xs)
    assert sorted(xs).count(0) == xs.count(0)   # every value's count is preserved
    assert len(sorted(xs)) == len(xs)            # nothing added or dropped
```

Hypothesis (Python) generates the input lists automatically — empty, single-element, all-duplicates, very long, negative numbers — and runs each property against all of them. No test author wrote `[]` or `[-5,-5,-5]` by hand; the framework found them because they're valid members of the input space the property claims to hold over.

slides.subTitle: From a 200-element failure to a 2-element repro
slides.markdown:
A property-based test that fails on a randomly generated input is only useful if you can understand *why* — and the framework's first failing case might be a 200-element list with arbitrary values, which is nearly impossible to debug by eye.

**Shrinking** solves this: once a failure is found, the framework automatically tries smaller, simpler variations of that same failing input — removing elements, replacing values with 0, halving the list — re-checking the property against each, and keeps the smallest one that still fails. The 200-element failure becomes a 2-element or 3-element minimal repro: `[0, -1]`, say, which immediately points at an off-by-one or sign-handling bug.

This is arguably the single feature that makes property-based testing practical rather than merely interesting — without shrinking, a failing property test hands you a haystack; with it, you get the needle.

**Fuzzing** shares property-based testing's core idea — generate inputs automatically rather than by hand — but with a different goal: not "does this invariant hold" but "can I make this crash, hang, or misbehave at all." Fuzzers feed malformed, truncated, oversized, or adversarially-mutated input directly at a parser, a file format reader, a network protocol handler — anywhere untrusted input reaches your code.

This is where a huge fraction of real security vulnerabilities are found in practice: buffer overflows, unhandled exceptions that crash a service, infinite loops on pathological input. Google's OSS-Fuzz project has found tens of thousands of bugs in open-source C/C++ projects this way, many of them genuine security holes that years of example-based tests and code review missed, because no human writer thought to try that specific malformed byte sequence.

Fuzzing and property-based testing are close cousins — both generate inputs automatically — but fuzzing's target is robustness against hostile input, not correctness against a defined invariant.

**Snapshot testing** takes a different approach entirely: instead of a human writing an expected output, the test captures the *actual* output once (a rendered UI component's markup, a serialized API response, generated code) and stores it as a **golden file**. Every future run compares fresh output against that stored baseline, character for character.

This is valuable exactly where writing an expected value by hand is impractical — a full HTML render, a large JSON payload, a compiler's generated output — but it inverts the usual test-writing relationship: nobody actually specified what "correct" looks like, they specified what the code *currently* produces. A snapshot test passes as long as output doesn't change, which is a useful regression signal, but it is fundamentally different from asserting the output is *right*.

| | Example-based | Property-based | Snapshot |
|---|---|---|---|
| What's specified | A specific input and its exact expected output | An invariant that must hold across generated inputs | Whatever the code currently outputs, captured once |
| Best at | Clear, known business rules and edge cases | Finding edge cases a human wouldn't think to write | Catching unintended changes in large, complex output |
| Blind to | Cases nobody thought to write | Invariants nobody thought to state | Whether the captured baseline was ever actually correct |
| Human effort per case | High — every case hand-written | Low per input, higher to design the property itself | Very low — just approve the diff |

None of the three is a replacement for the others — a mature suite layers them: example-based tests for known business rules, property-based tests for invariants over open-ended input spaces, snapshot tests for large structured output where hand-specifying every field isn't practical.

Snapshot testing's biggest risk is procedural, not technical: when a snapshot test fails, the fix is one command — `update-snapshots` — and under time pressure, engineers run it without carefully reviewing whether the *new* output is actually correct or just different. A snapshot diff showing forty changed lines of generated HTML is tedious to review line by line, so it gets approved on the assumption that "the change was intentional" without confirming the specific diff is right.

Once this becomes habitual, the test suite is testing nothing — every failure gets rubber-stamped into the new baseline regardless of whether it's correct, which means a snapshot test can be green for months while quietly "passing" a real regression that got approved without scrutiny the day it was introduced.

The mitigation: review every snapshot diff as carefully as a code review comment, treat a large or hard-to-parse diff as a signal the underlying output is too big to snapshot usefully (consider snapshotting a smaller, more targeted slice instead), and never bulk-approve a batch of snapshot changes without reading each one.

Reaching for property-based testing or fuzzing everywhere is itself a mistake — both have real setup cost (finding a good property is genuinely hard for code with complex business logic; a fuzzer needs a harness and time to run), and neither replaces example-based tests for clearly-specified business rules, where a human simply knows the right answer and writing it down is cheap.

The judgement call that separates strong candidates: reach for property-based testing where the input space is large and an invariant is genuinely easier to state than an exhaustive list of examples (serialization round-trips, sorting, parsers). Reach for fuzzing specifically at trust boundaries — anywhere untrusted or external input reaches your code. Reach for snapshot testing only for large structured output where hand-writing the expected value isn't practical, and only with a firm review discipline in place. None of the three should be the default for code with a small, well-understood set of cases.

This group started with why automated tests exist at all and the shape of the [test pyramid](testing-fundamentals-pyramid), moved through [unit tests](unit-testing-principles), [test doubles](test-doubles-mocking), [TDD](tdd-red-green-refactor), [integration](integration-testing) and [e2e testing](e2e-and-ui-testing), then [coverage](code-coverage-and-test-quality) and [suite strategy at scale](test-strategy-at-scale). Property-based and specialized testing close the loop: even a well-organized, fast, non-flaky suite built entirely from human-written examples has a ceiling — it only ever checks what a human thought to check.

The strongest test strategies combine both worlds: the judgment and domain knowledge of hand-written example tests, plus the tireless, unimaginative thoroughness of a generator that will happily try the input a human never would.
